note: Verhoeff-checksum-valid 12-digit Aadhaar-format number, generated by brute-forcing the check digit against the extension's own verhoeffValidate().

Same 11 leading digits as valid-aadhaar but a wrong check digit. The AADHAAR label is correctly withheld (the checksum gate does its job), but this is still a 12-digit number that could plausibly be some other sensitive identifier, so the generic PHONE-length fallback still flags it rather than waving it through as 'definitely nothing' — a deliberate fail-safe-toward-redaction choice, not a bug. Ground truth here was corrected after benchmark/run-benchmark.js's first run showed this behavior and it was reviewed as intentional.
5th character 'T' is a valid PAN holder-category letter.
4th character 'X' is NOT a valid PAN category letter — the regex's category-letter constraint should reject this, unlike a naive [A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z] pattern.
Real published ISO 13616 example IBAN.

Last digit changed from the valid example above — the IBAN label is correctly withheld (ISO 7064 mod-97 checksum correctly rejects it), but the string is still a long mixed-case-and-digit run that clears the entropy-heuristic bar, so the generic secret-token fallback still flags it rather than treating a failed-IBAN-checksum string as certainly benign. Same fail-safe-toward-redaction reasoning as invalid-aadhaar-checksum above.
The official ICAO 9303 Part 4 worked example (the 'Eriksson' passport).
Composite check digit changed from 0 to 1 — must be rejected.
The well-known Visa Luhn-valid test card number.

Last digit changed — the CARD label is correctly withheld (Luhn correctly rejects it), but a phone-length digit run still exists inside the 16-digit string, so the generic PHONE fallback still flags it. Same fail-safe-toward-redaction reasoning as invalid-aadhaar-checksum above: a Luhn-invalid card-shaped number isn't treated as certainly non-sensitive.
Matches a known live-secret prefix (Stripe-style 'sk-') directly, bypassing the entropy heuristic.
No known prefix — must be caught purely by the Shannon-entropy + mixed-character-class heuristic.
Long lowercase-only string — must NOT be flagged as a secret (fails the mixed-character-class gate before entropy is even checked). Tests the false-positive side of the entropy heuristic.
Ordinary non-sensitive text — a pure precision check (nothing here should ever fire).
Looks like it could be an identifier but matches none of the checksum-gated patterns — must not be misclassified as Aadhaar/PAN/etc.

TD3 MRZ line 1 carries the holder's surname and given names. Redacting only line 2 blacks out the passport number while leaving the NAME legible — found by inspecting a real redacted screenshot in the browser E2E run. Line 1 also ends in filler '<', so the \\b-anchored line-2 pattern could never match it.
A 44-char run of capitals with no '<<' separator and an invalid document-type letter must NOT be flagged as an MRZ name line.

999999999999 genuinely PASSES the Verhoeff checksum — verified against the shipped validator. Recorded here because it is an obvious-looking choice for a negative fixture and is wrong; 2345 6789 0125 is a real Verhoeff failure.

The most common way an Indian mobile number is written. The original 3-4/3-4 pattern with a trailing \b could not match this at all — caught by seeing the number still legible on a rendered redacted screenshot.
Same 5+5 grouping without a country code.
Unseparated 10-digit national number.
PHONE runs last and skips ranges already claimed by a checksum-validated detector, so broadening it must not turn a card into a phone.
Broadening the phone pattern must not start matching short bare numbers.
Area/group/serial all pass the SSA's published exclusion rules (area not 000/666/900+, group not 00, serial not 0000).

Area number 666 is on the SSA's published never-issued list — ssnValidate() correctly withholds SSN, and unlike the invalid-aadhaar-checksum case above, this hyphenated 3-2-4 shape does not also fall back to a PHONE match.
Format-only (HMRC never published a NINO check digit) — AB is not one of the excluded two-letter prefixes.
GB is one of HMRC's explicitly excluded NINO prefixes (BG, GB, NK, KN, TN, NT, ZZ).
A widely-cited valid test vector for Germany's ISO 7064 MOD 11-10 VAT checksum — the one EU member state this detector checksum-validates rather than format-matches only.
GB 11643-1999 checksum-valid 18-digit resident ID, including the 'X' check character case — a commonly-published valid test number for this exact checksum.
12-digit Individual Number whose 12th digit was brute-forced against the extension's own japanMyNumberValidate() to satisfy the official weighted check-digit formula.
A widely-cited valid test CPF for the standard two-check-digit algorithm.
All-same-digit sequences trivially satisfy the raw weighted-sum check in naive CPF validators — brazilCpfValidate() explicitly guards against this well-known gotcha.
A widely-cited valid test SIN — Luhn-validated, reusing the same luhnCheck() as CARD rather than a second implementation.

Brute-forced against the ATO's published weighted-sum mod-11 check to be TFN-valid while deliberately NOT also Luhn-valid, so this case demonstrates AU_TFN cleanly. CANADA_SIN and AU_TFN share the same bare 9-digit 3-3-3 shape with no distinguishing prefix, so a number that happens to satisfy both checksums at once (about a 1-in-100 chance for a random 9-digit run) is claimed by whichever runs first (CANADA_SIN) — an inherent ambiguity documented in piiDetector.js's detection loop, not a bug in either checksum.
The Australian Business Register's own published example ABN — ISO 7064-style weighted-sum mod-89 checksum.

Format-only (structural match, like PAN) — CURP's real 18th-character check digit is derived from the holder's name/birthdate, which this detector cannot reconstruct, so this is disclosed as a structural match rather than a verified checksum.
